claim: Sister chromatid cohesion is essential for mitotic chromosome segregation.
source: Sister chromatid cohesion essential for mitotic chromosome segregation is thought to involve the co-entrapment of sister DNAs within cohesin rings.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: Sister chromatid cohesion is thought to involve the co-entrapment of sister DNAs within cohesin rings.
source: Sister chromatid cohesion essential for mitotic chromosome segregation is thought to involve the co-entrapment of sister DNAs within cohesin rings.
evidence: This is presented as a prevailing hypothesis in the field.

claim: Cohesin can load onto chromosomes throughout the cell cycle.
source: Although cohesin can load onto chromosomes throughout the cell cycle, it only builds cohesion during S phase.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Cohesin only builds cohesion during S phase.
source: Although cohesin can load onto chromosomes throughout the cell cycle, it only builds cohesion during S phase.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, cohesion is generated by conversion of cohesin complexes associated with un-replicated DNAs ahead of replication forks into cohesive structures behind them.
source: We show here that in S. cerevisiae, both mechanisms exist and that each requires a different set of replisome-associated proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, cohesion is generated by de novo loading of nucleoplasmic cohesin onto nascent DNAs associated with forks.
source: We show here that in S. cerevisiae, both mechanisms exist and that each requires a different set of replisome-associated proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: Cohesion produced by cohesin conversion requires Tof1/Csm3, Ctf4 and Chl1 but not Scc2.
source: Cohesion produced by cohesin conversion requires Tof1/Csm3, Ctf4 and Chl1 but not Scc2 while that created by Scc2-dependent de novo loading at replication forks requires the Ctf18-RFC complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: Cohesion created by Scc2-dependent de novo loading at replication forks requires the Ctf18-RFC complex.
source: Cohesion produced by cohesin conversion requires Tof1/Csm3, Ctf4 and Chl1 but not Scc2 while that created by Scc2-dependent de novo loading at replication forks requires the Ctf18-RFC complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: Cohesin was initially identified as being necessary for sister chromatid cohesion.
source: Although initially identified as being necessary for sister chromatid cohesion (Guacci et al., 1997; Michaelis et al., 1997), cohesin also has a major role in organizing the topology of individual interphase chromatin fibres (Rao et al., 2017), a function thought to stem from its ability to trap and processively enlarge DNA loops (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cohesin has a major role in organizing the topology of individual interphase chromatin fibres.
source: Although initially identified as being necessary for sister chromatid cohesion (Guacci et al., 1997; Michaelis et al., 1997), cohesin also has a major role in organizing the topology of individual interphase chromatin fibres (Rao et al., 2017), a function thought to stem from its ability to trap and processively enlarge DNA loops (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cohesin's role in organizing chromatin topology is thought to stem from its ability to trap and processively enlarge DNA loops.
source: Although initially identified as being necessary for sister chromatid cohesion (Guacci et al., 1997; Michaelis et al., 1997), cohesin also has a major role in organizing the topology of individual interphase chromatin fibres (Rao et al., 2017), a function thought to stem from its ability to trap and processively enlarge DNA loops (Davidson et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cohesin contains a pair of rod-shaped SMC proteins (Smc1 and 3).
source: Like all other SMC protein complexes, cohesin contains a pair of rod-shaped SMC proteins (Smc1 and 3), whose association via their hinge domains creates V-shaped heterodimers with ATPase domains at their vertices that are interconnected by a kleisin subunit (Scc1) to form trimeric rings.
evidence: This is stated as established structural knowledge.

claim: SMC proteins associate via their hinge domains to create V-shaped heterodimers with ATPase domains at their vertices.
source: Like all other SMC protein complexes, cohesin contains a pair of rod-shaped SMC proteins (Smc1 and 3), whose association via their hinge domains creates V-shaped heterodimers with ATPase domains at their vertices that are interconnected by a kleisin subunit (Scc1) to form trimeric rings.
evidence: This is stated as established structural knowledge.

claim: SMC heterodimers are interconnected by a kleisin subunit (Scc1) to form trimeric rings.
source: Like all other SMC protein complexes, cohesin contains a pair of rod-shaped SMC proteins (Smc1 and 3), whose association via their hinge domains creates V-shaped heterodimers with ATPase domains at their vertices that are interconnected by a kleisin subunit (Scc1) to form trimeric rings.
evidence: This is stated as established structural knowledge.

claim: Cohesin trimers have little or no ATPase or loop extrusion activity in vitro.
source: These trimers have little or no ATPase or loop extrusion activity in vitro nor do they possess any biological function in vivo and require an additional set of proteins, namely a set of hook-shaped proteins composed of HEAT repeats known as HAWKs (HEAT repeat proteins Associated With Kleisins) (Wells et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cohesin trimers do not possess any biological function in vivo.
source: These trimers have little or no ATPase or loop extrusion activity in vitro nor do they possess any biological function in vivo and require an additional set of proteins, namely a set of hook-shaped proteins composed of HEAT repeats known as HAWKs (HEAT repeat proteins Associated With Kleisins) (Wells et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cohesin requires HAWKs (HEAT repeat proteins Associated With Kleisins) for function.
source: These trimers have little or no ATPase or loop extrusion activity in vitro nor do they possess any biological function in vivo and require an additional set of proteins, namely a set of hook-shaped proteins composed of HEAT repeats known as HAWKs (HEAT repeat proteins Associated With Kleisins) (Wells et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cohesin has three HAWKs: Scc3, Scc2/Nipbl, and Pds5.
source: Cohesin has three HAWKs: Scc3 is permanently bound while Scc2/Nipbl and Pds5 appear interchangeable (Petela et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Scc3 is permanently bound to cohesin.
source: Cohesin has three HAWKs: Scc3 is permanently bound while Scc2/Nipbl and Pds5 appear interchangeable (Petela et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Scc2/Nipbl and Pds5 appear interchangeable on cohesin.
source: Cohesin has three HAWKs: Scc3 is permanently bound while Scc2/Nipbl and Pds5 appear interchangeable (Petela et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cleavage of Scc1 by separase triggers cohesin's dissociation from chromosomes at the onset of anaphase.
source: Along with the finding that cleavage of Scc1 by separase triggers cohesin's dissociation from chromosomes as well as sister chromatid disjunction at the onset of anaphase (Oliveira et al., 2010; Uhlmann et al., 1999), the discovery that cohesin forms a tripartite ring raised the possibility that it holds DNAs together using a topological principle, by co-entrapment of sister DNAs within Smc-kleisin rings, a notion known as the ring model (Haering et al., 2002; Nasmyth, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cleavage of Scc1 by separase triggers sister chromatid disjunction at the onset of anaphase.
source: Along with the finding that cleavage of Scc1 by separase triggers cohesin's dissociation from chromosomes as well as sister chromatid disjunction at the onset of anaphase (Oliveira et al., 2010; Uhlmann et al., 1999), the discovery that cohesin forms a tripartite ring raised the possibility that it holds DNAs together using a topological principle, by co-entrapment of sister DNAs within Smc-kleisin rings, a notion known as the ring model (Haering et al., 2002; Nasmyth, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ring model proposes that cohesin holds DNAs together by co-entrapment of sister DNAs within Smc-kleisin rings.
source: Along with the finding that cleavage of Scc1 by separase triggers cohesin's dissociation from chromosomes as well as sister chromatid disjunction at the onset of anaphase (Oliveira et al., 2010; Uhlmann et al., 1999), the discovery that cohesin forms a tripartite ring raised the possibility that it holds DNAs together using a topological principle, by co-entrapment of sister DNAs within Smc-kleisin rings, a notion known as the ring model (Haering et al., 2002; Nasmyth, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Crosslinking all three interfaces of cohesin in living cells creates circular Smc1-Smc3-Scc1 polypeptides within which circular mini-chromosome DNAs can be entrapped in a manner resistant to SDS treatment.
source: As predicted by the ring model, crosslinking all three interfaces in living cells creates circular Smc1-Smc3-Scc1 polypeptides within which circular mini-chromosome DNAs would be entrapped in a manner resistant to SDS treatment.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Catenation by cohesin of individual DNAs modestly retards their electrophoretic migration (creating catenated monomers or CMs).
source: Catenation by cohesin of individual DNAs in this manner modestly retards their electrophoretic migration (creating catenated monomers or CMs) while co-entrapment of sister DNAs causes them to migrate as dimers (catenated dimers or CDs) even when they are not otherwise intertwined through DNA-DNA catenation (Gligoris et al., 2014; Haering et al., 2008; Srinivasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Co-entrapment of sister DNAs by cohesin causes them to migrate as dimers (catenated dimers or CDs) even when they are not otherwise intertwined through DNA-DNA catenation.
source: Catenation by cohesin of individual DNAs in this manner modestly retards their electrophoretic migration (creating catenated monomers or CMs) while co-entrapment of sister DNAs causes them to migrate as dimers (catenated dimers or CDs) even when they are not otherwise intertwined through DNA-DNA catenation (Gligoris et al., 2014; Haering et al., 2008; Srinivasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Strict topological entrapment of DNAs within cohesin rings is not essential for cohesin's association with yeast chromosomes in vivo.
source: Strict topological entrapment of DNAs within cohesin rings, as measured in the above manner, is not essential either for cohesin's association with yeast chromosomes in vivo (Srinivasan et al., 2018) or for loop extrusion by mammalian cohesin rings in vitro (Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Strict topological entrapment of DNAs within cohesin rings is not essential for loop extrusion by mammalian cohesin rings in vitro.
source: Strict topological entrapment of DNAs within cohesin rings, as measured in the above manner, is not essential either for cohesin's association with yeast chromosomes in vivo (Srinivasan et al., 2018) or for loop extrusion by mammalian cohesin rings in vitro (Davidson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cohesin is capable of entrapping individual DNAs prior to DNA replication.
source: Nevertheless, cohesin is capable of entrapping individual DNAs prior to DNA replication and also does so when expressed in post-replicative cells, where it is known to load onto chromosomes without forming sister chromatid cohesion (Srinivasan et al., 2019; Srinivasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cohesin entraps individual DNAs when expressed in post-replicative cells, where it loads onto chromosomes without forming sister chromatid cohesion.
source: Nevertheless, cohesin is capable of entrapping individual DNAs prior to DNA replication and also does so when expressed in post-replicative cells, where it is known to load onto chromosomes without forming sister chromatid cohesion (Srinivasan et al., 2019; Srinivasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CD formation accompanies the establishment of cohesion in all cases hitherto analysed.
source: In contrast, CD formation accompanies the establishment of cohesion in all cases hitherto analysed, suggesting that co-entrapment within cohesin's Smc-kleisin ring may indeed be the mechanism by which cohesin holds sister DNAs together.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior analyses.

claim: Co-entrapment within cohesin's Smc-kleisin ring may be the mechanism by which cohesin holds sister DNAs together.
source: In contrast, CD formation accompanies the establishment of cohesion in all cases hitherto analysed, suggesting that co-entrapment within cohesin's Smc-kleisin ring may indeed be the mechanism by which cohesin holds sister DNAs together.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on observations.

claim: The fraction of cohesin associated with chromatin is determined by its rate of association and its rate of dissociation.
source: Throughout most of the cell cycle, apart from anaphase when kleisin cleavage causes rapid dissociation, the fraction of cohesin associated with chromatin is determined by its rate of association and its rate of dissociation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Cohesin's rate of association depends on Scc2, Scc3, and Scc4.
source: The former depends on Scc2, Scc3, and Scc4, which binds to Scc2's N-terminal domain (Chao et al., 2015; Hinshaw et al., 2015; Kikuchi et al., 2016), while the latter depends on a regulatory subunit called Wapl, which binds to both Scc3 and Pds5 (Yatskevich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Scc4 binds to Scc2's N-terminal domain.
source: The former depends on Scc2, Scc3, and Scc4, which binds to Scc2's N-terminal domain (Chao et al., 2015; Hinshaw et al., 2015; Kikuchi et al., 2016), while the latter depends on a regulatory subunit called Wapl, which binds to both Scc3 and Pds5 (Yatskevich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cohesin's rate of dissociation depends on Wapl.
source: The former depends on Scc2, Scc3, and Scc4, which binds to Scc2's N-terminal domain (Chao et al., 2015; Hinshaw et al., 2015; Kikuchi et al., 2016), while the latter depends on a regulatory subunit called Wapl, which binds to both Scc3 and Pds5 (Yatskevich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Wapl binds to both Scc3 and Pds5.
source: The former depends on Scc2, Scc3, and Scc4, which binds to Scc2's N-terminal domain (Chao et al., 2015; Hinshaw et al., 2015; Kikuchi et al., 2016), while the latter depends on a regulatory subunit called Wapl, which binds to both Scc3 and Pds5 (Yatskevich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Scc2 is necessary for maintaining loop extrusion in vitro.
source: Scc2 is not merely a loading factor as it is also necessary for maintaining loop extrusion in vitro (Davidson et al., 2019) as well as cohesin's association with chromatin in vivo during G1 phase (Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Scc2 is necessary for cohesin's association with chromatin in vivo during G1 phase.
source: Scc2 is not merely a loading factor as it is also necessary for maintaining loop extrusion in vitro (Davidson et al., 2019) as well as cohesin's association with chromatin in vivo during G1 phase (Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Scc2 prevents dissociation of the Smc3/Scc1 interface.
source: In the latter case, it does so by preventing dissociation of the Smc3/Scc1 interface (Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The maintenance of sister chromatid cohesion depends on abrogation of Wapl-induced release through modification of K112 and K113 on Smc3 by the Eco1 acetyl transferase.
source: What is clear is that the maintenance of sister chromatid cohesion, once established during S phase, depends on abrogation of Wapl-induced release through modification of K112 and K113 on Smc3 by the Eco1 acetyl transferase (Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008; Ivanov et al., 2002; Unal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In yeast, Smc3 acetylation only takes place during S phase.
source: In yeast, acetylation only takes place during S phase and appears to be sufficient to block release (Beckouët et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In yeast, Smc3 acetylation appears to be sufficient to block Wapl-mediated release.
source: In yeast, acetylation only takes place during S phase and appears to be sufficient to block release (Beckouët et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In mammalian cells, Smc3 acetylation is necessary but insufficient to protect cohesion.
source: In mammalian cells, Smc3 acetylation, though necessary, is insufficient and the continual association of another factor named sororin is necessary to protect cohesive structures over the long term (Nishiyama et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In mammalian cells, the continual association of sororin is necessary to protect cohesive structures over the long term.
source: In mammalian cells, Smc3 acetylation, though necessary, is insufficient and the continual association of another factor named sororin is necessary to protect cohesive structures over the long term (Nishiyama et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Eco1 is required to build cohesion during S phase but not to maintain it during G2.
source: Because it is required to build cohesion during S phase but not to maintain it during G2 or indeed for cohesin's association with chromatin in the first place, Eco1 was initially thought to be intimately involved in the process by which cohesion is established (Toth et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Eco1 acetyl transferases are largely dispensable for building and maintaining sister chromatid cohesion in yeast cells lacking Wapl.
source: It is now appreciated that these acetyl transferases are merely needed to counteract Wapl-mediated release and as a consequence they are largely dispensable for building and maintaining sister chromatid cohesion in yeast (Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008; Chan et al., 2012; De et al., 2014; Feytout et al., 2011; Rowland et al., 2009; Srinivasan et al., 2018; Sutani et al., 2009), mammalian (Ladurner et al., 2016) or even plant cells (De et al., 2014) lacking Wapl.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Eco1 acetyl transferases are largely dispensable for building and maintaining sister chromatid cohesion in mammalian cells lacking Wapl.
source: It is now appreciated that these acetyl transferases are merely needed to counteract Wapl-mediated release and as a consequence they are largely dispensable for building and maintaining sister chromatid cohesion in yeast (Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008; Chan et al., 2012; De et al., 2014; Feytout et al., 2011; Rowland et al., 2009; Srinivasan et al., 2018; Sutani et al., 2009), mammalian (Ladurner et al., 2016) or even plant cells (De et al., 2014) lacking Wapl.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Eco1 acetyl transferases are largely dispensable for building and maintaining sister chromatid cohesion in plant cells lacking Wapl.
source: It is now appreciated that these acetyl transferases are merely needed to counteract Wapl-mediated release and as a consequence they are largely dispensable for building and maintaining sister chromatid cohesion in yeast (Rolef Ben-Shahar et al., 2008; Chan et al., 2012; De et al., 2014; Feytout et al., 2011; Rowland et al., 2009; Srinivasan et al., 2018; Sutani et al., 2009), mammalian (Ladurner et al., 2016) or even plant cells (De et al., 2014) lacking Wapl.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cohesin which loads onto chromosomes in post-replicative cells does not tether sister DNAs together.
source: An important finding is that cohesin which loads onto chromosomes in post-replicative cells does not tether sister DNAs together, even though it is capable of entrapping individual DNAs (Haering et al., 2004; Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The process of establishing cohesion appears to be confined to S phase.
source: The process of establishing cohesion appears therefore to be confined to S phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cohesin loaded in post-replicative cells does not form cohesion.

claim: Replication fork passage in mammalian cells does not cause dissociation of chromosomal cohesin in the absence of Wapl.
source: The first indication that chromosomal cohesin associated with un-replicated DNA can be 'converted' into cohesive structures was the observation that replication fork passage in mammalian cells does not cause dissociation of chromosomal cohesin, at least in the absence of Wapl (Rhodes et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Separase resistant cohesin complexes loaded onto yeast mini-chromosomes during G2 remain associated with chromatin and are converted into cohesive structures upon a round of re-replication induced by the transient inhibition of Cdk1.
source: More recently, we have shown that separase resistant cohesin complexes loaded onto yeast mini-chromosomes during G2 remain associated with chromatin and are converted into cohesive structures upon a round of re-replication induced by the transient inhibition of Cdk1. (Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cohesin conversion occurs even when Scc2 has been inactivated after the initial loading during G2.
source: Crucially, this occurs even when Scc2 has been inactivated after the initial loading during G2, suggesting that cohesin is converted into cohesive structures without any further participation of Scc2 (Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Numerous proteins associated with replisomes have important albeit non-essential roles in cohesion establishment.
source: The notion that cohesion might be established during S phase by two different pathways is consistent with the finding that numerous proteins associated with replisomes, namely Ctf4 (Hanna et al., 2001), Chl1 (Petronczki et al., 2004; Skibbens, 2004), the Csm3/Tof1 complex (Mayer et al., 2004), Mrc1 (Xu et al., 2004), and the Ctf18-RFC Mayer et al., 2001 have important albeit non-essential roles in cohesion establishment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

source: The notion that cohesion might be established during S phase by two different pathways is consistent with the finding that numerous proteins associated with replisomes, namely Ctf4 (Hanna et al., 2001), Chl1 (Petronczki et al., 2004; Skibbens, 2004), the Csm3/Tof1 complex (Mayer et al., 2004), Mrc1 (Xu et al., 2004), and the Ctf18-RFC Mayer et al., 2001 have important albeit non-essential roles in cohesion establishment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Csm3/Tof1 complex has an important albeit non-essential role in cohesion establishment.
source: The notion that cohesion might be established during S phase by two different pathways is consistent with the finding that numerous proteins associated with replisomes, namely Ctf4 (Hanna et al., 2001), Chl1 (Petronczki et al., 2004; Skibbens, 2004), the Csm3/Tof1 complex (Mayer et al., 2004), Mrc1 (Xu et al., 2004), and the Ctf18-RFC Mayer et al., 2001 have important albeit non-essential roles in cohesion establishment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

source: The notion that cohesion might be established during S phase by two different pathways is consistent with the finding that numerous proteins associated with replisomes, namely Ctf4 (Hanna et al., 2001), Chl1 (Petronczki et al., 2004; Skibbens, 2004), the Csm3/Tof1 complex (Mayer et al., 2004), Mrc1 (Xu et al., 2004), and the Ctf18-RFC Mayer et al., 2001 have important albeit non-essential roles in cohesion establishment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Replisome-associated proteins implicated in cohesion establishment belong to two epistasis groups: one containing Chl1, Ctf4, Csm3 and Tof1 and a second containing Mrc1 as well as Ctf8, Ctf18, and Dcc1.
source: A comprehensive analysis of the viability of double mutant strains as well as their sister chromatid cohesion implied that these genes/proteins belong to two epistasis groups, one containing Chl1, Ctf4, Csm3 and Tof1 and a second containing Mrc1 as well as Ctf8, Ctf18, and Dcc1, which are all subunits of the Ctf18-RFC (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Combining two mutants from the same epistasis group has little or no additional effect on viability and causes no greater cohesion defect than the single mutants.
source: Thus, combining two mutants from the first group or from the second group has little or no additional effect on viability and causes no greater cohesion defect than the single mutants, while combining mutants from different groups either causes lethality or synthetic sickness and, when measured using conditional alleles, greatly increased defects in sister chromatid cohesion (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1B and citation to prior work.

claim: Combining mutants from different epistasis groups either causes lethality or synthetic sickness and greatly increased defects in sister chromatid cohesion.
source: Thus, combining two mutants from the first group or from the second group has little or no additional effect on viability and causes no greater cohesion defect than the single mutants, while combining mutants from different groups either causes lethality or synthetic sickness and, when measured using conditional alleles, greatly increased defects in sister chromatid cohesion (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1B and citation to prior work.

claim: None of the replisome proteins (Ctf4, Chl1, Csm3/Tof1, Mrc1, Ctf18-RFC) are necessary for DNA replication.
source: Although none of these proteins are necessary for DNA replication, all are associated with the replisome, suggesting that their role is to establish cohesion during S phase.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: All replisome proteins (Ctf4, Chl1, Csm3/Tof1, Mrc1, Ctf18-RFC) are associated with the replisome.
source: Although none of these proteins are necessary for DNA replication, all are associated with the replisome, suggesting that their role is to establish cohesion during S phase.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Inactivation of conditional alleles of replisome proteins during G2/M has no effect on the maintenance of cohesion once established.
source: Accordingly, inactivation of conditional alleles during G2/M has no effect on the maintenance of cohesion once established (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Expression of Chl1 during G2/M cannot rescue the cohesion defects caused by replication in its absence.
source: Moreover, expression of Chl1 during G2/M cannot rescue the cohesion defects caused by replication in its absence (Petronczki et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: All replisome proteins implicated in cohesion establishment are highly conserved among eukaryotes.
source: Though not essential, all of these replisome proteins are highly conserved among eukaryotes and aid cohesion establishment in human as well as yeast cells (Cortone et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Replisome proteins implicated in cohesion establishment aid cohesion establishment in human as well as yeast cells.
source: Though not essential, all of these replisome proteins are highly conserved among eukaryotes and aid cohesion establishment in human as well as yeast cells (Cortone et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 are essential for converting cohesin associated with un-replicated DNA into cohesive structures holding together sister DNAs.
source: We show here that Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 are essential for converting cohesin associated with un-replicated DNA into cohesive structures holding together sister DNAs, whereas Mrc1 and Ctf18-RFC are not.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: Mrc1 and Ctf18-RFC are not essential for converting cohesin associated with un-replicated DNA into cohesive structures.
source: We show here that Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 are essential for converting cohesin associated with un-replicated DNA into cohesive structures holding together sister DNAs, whereas Mrc1 and Ctf18-RFC are not.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: Cohesin conversion mediated by Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 is independent of Scc2.
source: Crucially, cohesin conversion mediated by Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 is independent of Scc2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: Ctf18-RFC is required for cohesion established through de novo loading at forks.
source: We present evidence that Ctf18-RFC is instead required for cohesion established through de novo loading at forks and show that this Scc2-dependent process (but not cohesin conversion) is enhanced by modest over-expression of Scc2/4.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: The Scc2-dependent de novo loading process (but not cohesin conversion) is enhanced by modest over-expression of Scc2/4.
source: We present evidence that Ctf18-RFC is instead required for cohesion established through de novo loading at forks and show that this Scc2-dependent process (but not cohesin conversion) is enhanced by modest over-expression of Scc2/4.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data.

claim: Scc2 is essential for de novo loading during S phase.
source: To exclude any possibility of cohesion being generated from cohesin loaded during the process of DNA replication, we needed to test its dependence on Scc2, which is essential for de novo loading.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Scc2 is necessary for maintaining cohesin's stable DNA association during G1, even in cells lacking Wapl-dependent release.
source: However, doing this with endogenous wild type cohesin is not in fact possible because Scc2 is also necessary for maintaining cohesin's stable DNA association during G1, even in cells lacking Wapl-dependent release (Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inactivation of Scc2 during G1 causes cohesin to dissociate from chromosomes.
source: Thus, inactivation of Scc2 during G1 causes cohesin to dissociate from chromosomes, which is incompatible with observing its conversion into cohesive structures.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation.

claim: Cohesin expressed in post-replicative G2 cells can load onto chromosomes and entrap individual DNAs (CMs) but cannot form cohesion or entrap sister DNAs (CDs).
source: First, cohesin expressed in post-replicative G2 cells can load onto chromosomes and entrap individual DNAs (CMs) but cannot form cohesion or entrap sister DNAs (CDs) (Haering et al., 2004; Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cohesin loaded during G2/M does not require Scc2 to prevent its release from chromosomes.
source: Second, unlike cohesin loaded during G1, cohesin loaded during G2/M does not require Scc2 to prevent its release from chromosomes and remarkably this property is maintained when cells exit mitosis and enter a new G1 phase, as long as the kleisin subunits of the cohesin in question are refractory to separase-mediated cleavage, which would otherwise induce its destruction (Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cohesin loaded during G2/M maintains its Scc2-independent stability when cells exit mitosis and enter a new G1 phase, as long as the kleisin subunits are refractory to separase-mediated cleavage.
source: Second, unlike cohesin loaded during G1, cohesin loaded during G2/M does not require Scc2 to prevent its release from chromosomes and remarkably this property is maintained when cells exit mitosis and enter a new G1 phase, as long as the kleisin subunits of the cohesin in question are refractory to separase-mediated cleavage, which would otherwise induce its destruction (Srinivasan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Wild type and scc2-45 cells produce CDs in similar amounts when cohesin loaded during G2/M undergoes replication.
source: To measure the fate of this 2CScc1NC cohesin pool during DNA replication in the presence (SCC2) or absence (scc2-45) of Scc2 activity, both cultures were transferred to pheromone-free medium at 37°C, whereupon both sets of cells duplicated their genomes and produced CDs in similar amounts (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In scc2-45 cells, CD formation is accompanied by a reduction in the fraction of DNAs that formed CMs.
source: In the scc2-45 cells, this was accompanied by a reduction in the fraction of DNAs that formed CMs, raising the possibility that the CMs associated with un-replicated DNAs were converted to CDs upon replication.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Higher levels of CMs were observed in the SCC2 wild-type cells, suggesting that some de novo loading may occur.
source: Higher levels of CMs were observed in the SCC2 wild-type cells, suggesting that some de novo loading may occur, either during S phase or during the subsequent G2.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with an inference about de novo loading.

claim: Cohesin associated with un-replicated DNAs is converted to cohesive structures during S phase in the absence of Scc2.
source: We conclude that cohesin associated with un-replicated mini-chromosome DNAs is converted into cohesive structures during S phase in the absence of Scc2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: None of the deletions (mrc1Δ, chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, tof1Δ, ctf18Δ) affected CMs when endogenous 6C cohesin was expressed.
source: As expected, none of the deletions affected CMs but more remarkably none caused any appreciable reduction in CDs either (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: None of the deletions (mrc1Δ, chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, tof1Δ, ctf18Δ) caused any appreciable reduction in CDs when endogenous 6C cohesin was expressed.
source: As expected, none of the deletions affected CMs but more remarkably none caused any appreciable reduction in CDs either (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All six deletions (mrc1Δ, chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, tof1Δ, ctf18Δ) cause modest but reproducible cohesion defects when cohesion of an individual chromosomal locus marked by GFP is measured.
source: When cohesion of an individual chromosomal locus marked by GFP is measured, all six deletions cause modest but reproducible cohesion defects (Borges et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2007), suggesting that the 6C mini-chromosome assay is less sensitive to minor cohesion establishment defects than GFP-based cytological assays.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The 6C mini-chromosome assay is less sensitive to minor cohesion establishment defects than GFP-based cytological assays.
source: When cohesion of an individual chromosomal locus marked by GFP is measured, all six deletions cause modest but reproducible cohesion defects (Borges et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2007), suggesting that the 6C mini-chromosome assay is less sensitive to minor cohesion establishment defects than GFP-based cytological assays.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of results between different assays.

claim: ctf18Δ and mrc1Δ cells formed CDs in a manner similar if not identical to wild type when cohesin loaded during G2/M underwent replication.
source: When allowed to undergo DNA replication upon release from the pheromone-induced G1 arrest (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), ctf18Δ and mrc1Δ cells formed CDs in a manner similar if not identical to wild type (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ cells produced no CDs when cohesin loaded during G2/M underwent replication.
source: Remarkably, the behaviour of chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ cells was completely different. No CDs were produced and most but not all CMs disappeared, as did most monomeric supercoils associated in a non-topological fashion with 2CScc1NC cohesin (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ cells, most but not all CMs disappeared when cohesin loaded during G2/M underwent replication.
source: Remarkably, the behaviour of chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ cells was completely different. No CDs were produced and most but not all CMs disappeared, as did most monomeric supercoils associated in a non-topological fashion with 2CScc1NC cohesin (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 (but not Ctf18-RFC) are essential for converting cohesin associated with un-replicated mini-chromosomes into cohesive structures as measured by CDs.
source: These data suggest that Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 (but not Ctf18-RFC) are essential for converting cohesin associated with un-replicated mini-chromosomes into cohesive structures as measured by CDs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Chl1, Ctf4, Csm3/Tof1 are necessary for preventing cohesin's dissociation from chromosomes during the passage from G1 to G2.
source: Equally surprising, these replisome proteins are also necessary for preventing cohesin's dissociation from chromosomes during the passage from G1 to G2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The division of replisome proteins into a group (containing Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1) required for conversion and one (containing Mrc1 and Ctf18-RFC) that is not, corresponds precisely with the two epistasis groups defined by the effects of double mutations on cohesion and viability.
source: It is remarkable that their division into a group (containing Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1) required for conversion and one (containing Mrc1 and Ctf18-RFC) that is not, corresponds precisely with the two epistasis groups defined by the effects of double mutations on cohesion and viability (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings with prior work.

claim: Chl1, Ctf4, Csm3/Tof1 form a single epistasis group because they are all concerned with conversion of pre-existing chromosomal cohesin into cohesive structures.
source: Our data suggest that Chl1, Ctf4, Csm3/Tof1 form a single epistasis group because they are all concerned with a very specific physiological function, namely conversion of pre-existing chromosomal cohesin into cohesive structures.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Conversion is not the sole mechanism by which cohesion is established during S phase.
source: An important corollary of our finding that Chl1, Ctf4, Csm3/Tof1 are essential for conversion (Figure 3B) but not for building cohesion per se (Figure 3A) or for cell proliferation, is that conversion is not the sole mechanism by which cohesion is established during S phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: A second mechanism involving Mrc1 and Ctf18-RFC is capable of generating cohesion in the complete absence of conversion.
source: As implied by the synthetic lethality caused by combining mutants from different epistasis groups (Xu et al., 2007) and as will become more apparent below, a second mechanism involving Mrc1 and Ctf18-RFC is capable of generating cohesion in the complete absence of conversion.
evidence: This is inferred from the synthetic lethality data and the current findings.

claim: A low but significant level of CMs can be detected in chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ mutant cells once they reach G2/M.
source: Although no CDs are formed and few CMs retained when chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ mutants undergo S phase, a low but significant level of CMs can nevertheless be detected in the mutant cells once they reach G2/M (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Combining scc2-45 with chl1Δ causes synthetic sickness.
source: When constructing these strains, we found that combining scc2-45 with chl1Δ caused synthetic sickness (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both wild type and scc2-45 cells produced CDs from 2CScc1NC cohesin loaded during the previous G2/M.
source: As expected, both wild type and scc2-45 cells produced CDs from 2CScc1NC cohesin loaded during the previous G2/M while neither chl1Δ, nor scc2-45 chl1Δ cells did so (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Neither chl1Δ nor scc2-45 chl1Δ cells produced CDs from 2CScc1NC cohesin loaded during the previous G2/M.
source: As expected, both wild type and scc2-45 cells produced CDs from 2CScc1NC cohesin loaded during the previous G2/M while neither chl1Δ, nor scc2-45 chl1Δ cells did so (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A small fraction of CMs and free supercoiled monomers associated with 2CScc1NC cohesin persisted in chl1Δ but none in scc2-45 chl1Δ cells after S phase.
source: Crucially, a small fraction of CMs and free supercoiled monomers associated with 2CScc1NC cohesin persisted in chl1Δ but none in scc2-45 chl1Δ cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 are important for maintaining cohesin on mini-chromosome DNA during S phase.
source: We conclude that Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 are important for maintaining cohesin on mini-chromosome DNA during S phase and that the low levels that do persist (at least in chl1Δ cells) arise from Scc2-dependent re-loading, either during or following passage through S phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The low levels of cohesin that persist in chl1Δ cells arise from Scc2-dependent re-loading, either during or following passage through S phase.
source: We conclude that Chl1, Ctf4, and Csm3/Tof1 are important for maintaining cohesin on mini-chromosome DNA during S phase and that the low levels that do persist (at least in chl1Δ cells) arise from Scc2-dependent re-loading, either during or following passage through S phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Scc1NC cohesin (loaded during the previous G2/M at 25°C) persisted throughout the genome during passage from G1 to G2 at 37°C in both wild type and scc2-45 cells.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Srinivasan et al., 2019), Scc1NC cohesin (loaded during the previous G2/M at 25°C) persisted throughout the genome during passage from G1 to G2 at 37°C in both wild type and scc2-45 cells. (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Half or more Scc1NC cohesin (loaded during the previous G2/M at 25°C) disappeared from all parts of genome when chl1Δ cells underwent S phase.
source: In contrast, half or more Scc1NC cohesin (loaded during the previous G2/M at 25°C) disappeared from all parts of genome when chl1Δ cells underwent S phase (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Nearly all pre-existing chromosomal Scc1NC cohesin disappeared during the passage from G1 to G2 in chl1Δ scc2-45 double mutant cells.
source: This effect that was even more pronounced in chl1Δ scc2-45 double mutant cells, which cannot reload cohesin during S phase, where nearly all pre-existing chromosomal Scc1NC cohesin disappeared during the passage from G1 to G2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Chl1 is essential for maintaining cohesin's association with the entire genome as cells undergo S phase.
source: We conclude that in addition to being required to build CDs from cohesin associated with un-replicated DNAs, Chl1 is essential for maintaining cohesin's association with the entire genome as cells undergo S phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: When expressed during S phase, 2CScc1NC can generate CDs in wild type and chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ mutant cells.
source: To address whether this discrepancy could be an artefact caused by the mutations that prevent 2CScc1NC's cleavage, we synchronised wild type, chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ cells in G1 and then allowed them to undergo S phase in the presence of galactose to induce 2CScc1NC. Under these circumstances, CD formation was identical in wild type and mutant cells (Figure 5A), proving that it is the time of synthesis and not whether it is non-cleavable that determines whether Scc1 can generate CDs in chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ mutant cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: It is the time of synthesis and not whether Scc1 is non-cleavable that determines whether Scc1 can generate CDs in chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ mutant cells.
source: Under these circumstances, CD formation was identical in wild type and mutant cells (Figure 5A), proving that it is the time of synthesis and not whether it is non-cleavable that determines whether Scc1 can generate CDs in chl1Δ, ctf4Δ, csm3Δ, and tof1Δ mutant cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: chl1Δ cells produced both CMs and CDs when 2CScc1NC was continuously expressed during S phase.
source: As expected, chl1Δ cells produced both CMs and CDs.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Neither CDs nor CMs nor any other form of interaction between 2CScc1NC cohesin and DNA was observed in chl1Δ scc2-45 cells when 2CScc1NC was continuously expressed during S phase at 37°C.
source: In contrast, neither CDs nor CMs nor any other form of interaction between 2CScc1NC cohesin and DNA was observed in chl1Δ scc2-45 cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The de novo pathway requires Scc2.
source: We conclude that the de novo pathway requires Scc2, which is not particularly surprising as it has long been known that Scc2 is required for endogenous nucleoplasmic cohesin to load onto chromosomes when G1 cells undergo S phase (Ciosk et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with support from prior work.

claim: Deleting MRC1 or CTF18 in chl1Δ mutants causes extreme sickness or lethality.
source: Indeed, we confirmed by tetrad analysis that deleting MRC1 or CTF18 in chl1Δ mutants does indeed cause extreme sickness or lethality (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CDs were formed efficiently in chl1Δ cells but barely if at all in the chl1Δ ctf8-17 double mutants when 2CScc1NC was continuously expressed during S phase at 37°C.
source: CDs were formed efficiently in chl1Δ cells but barely if at all in the chl1Δ ctf8-17 double mutants (Figure 5C) despite their completing DNA replication (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CM formation was unaffected by the ctf8-17 mutation in chl1Δ cells.
source: Although CD formation was abrogated by the ctf8-17 mutation, CM formation was unaffected, as were all forms of association between cohesin and mini-chromosome DNA, implying that Scc2 remains active in the chl1Δ ctf8-17 double mutant cells and loads cohesin onto individual DNA molecules either during or after replication (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Scc2 remains active in the chl1Δ ctf8-17 double mutant cells and loads cohesin onto individual DNA molecules either during or after replication.
source: Although CD formation was abrogated by the ctf8-17 mutation, CM formation was unaffected, as were all forms of association between cohesin and mini-chromosome DNA, implying that Scc2 remains active in the chl1Δ ctf8-17 double mutant cells and loads cohesin onto individual DNA molecules either during or after replication (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CM formation was unaffected.

claim: Scc2 cannot load cohesin onto nascent DNAs in a manner that entraps them inside the same cohesin ring in chl1Δ ctf8-17 double mutant cells.
source: Crucially, it cannot load cohesin onto nascent DNAs in a manner that entraps them inside the same cohesin ring.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Establishment of cohesion by the de novo pathway depends on the Ctf18-RFC complex.
source: We conclude that establishment of cohesion by the de novo pathway depends not only on Scc2 but also on the Ctf18-RFC complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There are only two pathways capable of creating CDs during S phase.
source: A corollary is that there are only two pathways capable of creating CDs during S phase and inactivation of both causes a loss of cohesion so complete that it causes lethality (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Inactivation of both cohesion establishment pathways causes a loss of cohesion so complete that it causes lethality.
source: A corollary is that there are only two pathways capable of creating CDs during S phase and inactivation of both causes a loss of cohesion so complete that it causes lethality (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CHL1 was identified as a multicopy suppressor of the poor spore viability of ctf8Δ cells.
source: Interestingly, CHL1 was identified as a multicopy suppressor of the poor spore viability of ctf8Δ cells (Petronczki et al., 2004), suggesting that it may be the rate-limiting factor of the conversion pathway and that the augmentation of conversion pathway by Chl1 over-expression can compensate for defects in the de novo pathway (due to ctf8Δ), at least during meiosis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Chl1 may be the rate-limiting factor of the conversion pathway.
source: Interestingly, CHL1 was identified as a multicopy suppressor of the poor spore viability of ctf8Δ cells (Petronczki et al., 2004), suggesting that it may be the rate-limiting factor of the conversion pathway and that the augmentation of conversion pathway by Chl1 over-expression can compensate for defects in the de novo pathway (due to ctf8Δ), at least during meiosis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the suppression data.

claim: Augmentation of conversion pathway by Chl1 over-expression can compensate for defects in the de novo pathway (due to ctf8Δ), at least during meiosis.
source: Interestingly, CHL1 was identified as a multicopy suppressor of the poor spore viability of ctf8Δ cells (Petronczki et al., 2004), suggesting that it may be the rate-limiting factor of the conversion pathway and that the augmentation of conversion pathway by Chl1 over-expression can compensate for defects in the de novo pathway (due to ctf8Δ), at least during meiosis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the suppression data.

claim: Introduction of CHL1 on the 2-micron vector caused a marked reduction in precocious sister chromatid separation from 47% to 18% in ctf8Δ cells.
source: In contrast, introduction of CHL1 on the 2-micron vector caused a marked reduction from 47% to 18% in ctf8Δ cells but a much more modest effect, from 49% to 40%, in ctf4Δ cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Introduction of CHL1 on the 2-micron vector caused a modest reduction in precocious sister chromatid separation from 49% to 40% in ctf4Δ cells.
source: In contrast, introduction of CHL1 on the 2-micron vector caused a marked reduction from 47% to 18% in ctf8Δ cells but a much more modest effect, from 49% to 40%, in ctf4Δ cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Augmentation of the conversion pathway by CHL1 over-expression can compensate for defects in the de novo pathway in mitotic cells as well as meiotic ones.
source: These data suggest that augmentation of the conversion pathway by CHL1 over-expression can compensate for defects in the de novo pathway in mitotic cells as well as meiotic ones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: CHL1 over-expression does not compensate for defective conversion caused by ctf4Δ.
source: Importantly, it does not compensate for defective conversion caused by ctf4Δ.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Chl1's association with chromatin depends on Ctf4.
source: Because Ctf4 remains important for conversion even when CHL1 is over-expressed, the ability of Chl1 to promote conversion depends on Ctf4's association with the replisome, which is consistent with the suggestion that Chl1's association with chromatin depends on Ctf4 (Samora et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: The reduced fitness of ctf4Δ relative to wildtype cells is partially suppressed by duplication of two different portions of the genome that contain the SCC2 and SCC4 genes.
source: It was recently reported that the reduced fitness of ctf4Δ relative to the wildtype cells is partially suppressed by duplication of two different portions of the genome that contain the SCC2 and SCC4 genes.
evidence: This is supported by reference to recent work.

claim: An extra copy merely of SCC2 partially ameliorates the cohesion defect of ctf4Δ cells.
source: Indeed, an extra copy merely of SCC2 partially ameliorates their cohesion defect (Fumasoni and Murray, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Increased Scc2/4 activity enhances establishment of cohesion by a Ctf4-independent pathway, presumably the de novo loading pathway dependent on Ctf18-RFC.
source: This finding implies not only that the cohesion defect contributes to the reduced fitness but also that increased Scc2/4 activity enhances establishment of cohesion by a Ctf4-independent pathway, presumably the de novo loading pathway dependent on Ctf18-RFC.
evidence: This is inferred from the suppression data.

claim: An additional copy of SCC2 increased the fitness of ctf4Δ cells.
source: Crucially, an additional copy of SCC2 increased the fitness of ctf4Δ (Figure 6B and Source data 1) but not that of ctf18Δ cells (Figure 6B and Source data 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: An additional copy of SCC2 did not increase the fitness of ctf18Δ cells.
source: Crucially, an additional copy of SCC2 increased the fitness of ctf4Δ (Figure 6B and Source data 1) but not that of ctf18Δ cells (Figure 6B and Source data 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Increased Scc2/4 levels suppresses ctf4Δ because it specifically enhances the Scc2-dependent de novo loading cohesion establishment pathway.
source: This is consistent with the notion that increased Scc2/4 levels suppresses ctf4Δ because it specifically enhances the Scc2-dependent de novo loading cohesion establishment pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Establishment of cohesion via the de novo loading pathway but not that of conversion is specifically augmented by modest over-expression of Scc2.
source: Thus, establishment of cohesion via the de novo loading pathway but not that of conversion is specifically augmented by modest over-expression of Scc2 while cohesion established by the conversion pathway is augmented by CHL1 over-expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Cohesion established by the conversion pathway is augmented by CHL1 over-expression.
source: Thus, establishment of cohesion via the de novo loading pathway but not that of conversion is specifically augmented by modest over-expression of Scc2 while cohesion established by the conversion pathway is augmented by CHL1 over-expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Augmentation of either pathway suppresses the reduction in cohesion establishment caused by abrogation of the other.
source: Importantly, augmentation of either pathway in this manner suppresses the reduction in cohesion establishment caused by abrogation of the other.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Sister DNAs generated during DNA replication must be held together from S phase until anaphase.
source: Sister DNAs generated during DNA replication must be held together from S phase until anaphase, when they finally disjoin to opposite poles of the cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The establishment of sister chromatid cohesion during S phase and its destruction during anaphase are aspects of chromosome biology unique to eukaryotic cells.
source: While there are similarities in the way bacteria and eukaryotes replicate their genomes, the establishment of sister chromatid cohesion during S phase and its destruction during anaphase are aspects of chromosome biology unique to eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Cohesion is mediated by cohesin, which belongs to one of three classes of eukaryotic SMC-kleisin protein containing complexes.
source: Cohesion is mediated by cohesin, which belongs to one of three classes of eukaryotic SMC-kleisin protein containing complexes (Yatskevich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cohesin associated with un-replicated DNA is converted into cohesive structures behind replication forks.
source: Figure 1A
evidence: This is depicted in Figure 1A as one of two mechanisms for cohesion establishment.

claim: Cohesion is built by de novo loading of cohesin molecules onto nascent DNAs at the replication forks.
source: Figure 1A
evidence: This is depicted in Figure 1A as one of two mechanisms for cohesion establishment.

claim: The median level of Scc1NC across the entire chromosome IV did not alter while cells remained blocked for an extended period in G1.
source: Moreover, calibrated ChIP sequencing showed that although there were variations in cohesin occupancy along the chromosomes, presumably due to cohesin re-localization, the median level of association along the entire genome of this pool of cohesin did not alter while cells remained blocked for an extended period in G1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The constant level of chromosomal 2CScc1NC cohesin during the G1 arrest implies that the G1 cells inherit little or no free nucleoplasmic 2CScc1NC cohesin that could load onto DNA during this period.
source: Because Wapl-mediated release is abrogated in these cells and because there is no further synthesis from the GAL promoter, the constant level of chromosomal 2CScc1NC cohesin during the arrest implies that the G1 cells inherit little or no free nucleoplasmic 2CScc1NC cohesin that could load onto DNA during this period.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of constant cohesin levels.

claim: Mini-chromosomes are merely 2.3 kb in length and contain CENs that act as potent cohesin loading sites.
source: We suggest that this difference may arise because mini-chromosomes are merely 2.3 kb in length and contain CENs that act as potent cohesin loading sites (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a property of mini-chromosomes with citation to prior work.

claim: Cells lacking individual members of the set of non-essential replisome associated proteins are perfectly capable of generating and maintaining cohesion of the mini-chromosomes when Scc1 expressed from its endogenous promoter can be loaded throughout G1 and S phase.
source: Crucially, cells lacking individual members of the above set of non-essential replisome associated proteins are perfectly capable of generating and maintaining cohesion of the mini-chromosomes, as measured by CD formation, when Scc1 expressed from its endogenous promoter can be loaded throughout G1 and S phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.
